'''''Eucalyptus rubida''''', commonly known as '''candlebark''', '''ribbon gum''' or '''white gum''',<ref name="CANBR">{{cite web |title=''Eucalyptus rubida'' subsp. ''rubida'' |url=https://apps.lucidcentral.org/euclid/text/entities/eucalyptus_rubida_subsp._rubida.htm |publisher=Euclid:Centre for Australian National Biodiversity Research |access-date=29 May 2020}}</ref> is a species of small to medium-sized tree that is [[Endemism|endemic]] to south-eastern [[Australia]]. It has smooth bark, sometimes with rough bark at the base, lance-shaped or curved adult leaves, flower buds in groups of three, white flowers and cup-shaped, hemispherical or bell-shaped fruit.

==Description==
''Eucalyptus rubida'' is a tree that typically grows to a height of {{cvt|20-40|m}} and forms a [[lignotuber]]. It has smooth, powdery, greyish or pink bark that is shed in long ribbons but there is sometimes persistent fibrous bark near the base of the trunk. Young plants and [[coppice]] regrowth have [[Sessility (botany)|sessile]], [[wikt:glaucous#Adjective|glaucous]], more or less round leaves {{cvt|2-6|mm}} wide arranged in opposite pairs. Adult leaves are arranged alternately, lance-shaped to curved, {{cvt|80-175|mm}} long and {{cvt|8-34|mm}} wide, tapering to a [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]] {{cvt|10-35|mm}} long. The flower buds are arranged in leaf [[wikt:axil|axil]]s in groups of three on an unbranched [[Peduncle (botany)|peduncle]], the individual buds sessile or an [[Pedicel (botany)|pedicels]] up to {{cvt|4|mm}} long. Mature buds are oval to spindle-shaped, {{cvt|5-9|mm}} long and {{cvt|3-5|mm}} wide with a conical to rounded [[Operculum (botany)|operculum]]. Flowering mainly occurs from December to April and the flowers are white. The fruit is a woody cup-shaped, hemispherical or bell-shaped [[Capsule (botany)|capsule]] {{cvt|3-6|mm}} long and {{cvt|4-8|mm}} wide with the valves near rim level or protruding slightly.<ref name="CANBR" /><ref name="RBGS">{{cite web |last1=Hill |first1=Ken |title=''Eucalyptus rubida'' |url=http://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Eucalyptus~rubida |publisher=Royal Botanic Garden Sydney |access-date=16 December 2019}}</ref><ref name="RBGV">{{cite web |title=''Eucalyptus rubida'' |url=https://vicflora.rbg.vic.gov.au/flora/taxon/58d1f64f-8724-428f-8c72-f9608e919e6c |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria |access-date=16 December 2019}}</ref><ref name="ABRS">{{cite web |last1=Chippendale |first1=George M. |title=''Eucalyptus rubida'' |url=https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Eucalyptus%20rubida |publisher=Australian Biological Resources Study, Department of the Environment and Energy, Canberra |access-date=16 December 2019}}</ref>

==Taxonomy and naming==
''Eucalyptus rubida'' was first formally described in 1899 by [[Henry Deane (engineer)|Henry Deane]] and [[Joseph Maiden]] in ''[[Linnean Society of New South Wales|Proceedings of the Linnean Society of New South Wales]]''.<ref name=APNI>{{cite web|title=''Eucalyptus rubida''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/454522|publisher=APNI|access-date=16 December 2019}}</ref><ref name="Deane">{{cite journal |last1=Deane |first1=Henry |last2=Maiden |first2=Joseph |title=Observations on the eucalypts of New South Wales, Part V |journal=Proceedings of the Linnean Society of New South Wales |date=1899 |volume=24 |issue=3 |pages=456–458 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/21735#page/554/mode/1up |access-date=16 December 2019}}</ref> The [[Botanical name|specific epithet]] (''rubida'') is from the [[Latin]] word ''rubidus'' meaning "red", referring to the seasonally red bark.<ref name="CANBR" />

In 1991, [[Lawrence Alexander Sidney Johnson|Lawrie Johnson]] and [[Ken Hill (botanist)|Ken Hill]] described two subspecies and the names are accepted by the [[Australian Plant Census]] as at December 2019:<ref name="Telopea">{{cite journal |last1=Johnson |first1=Lawrence A.S. |last2=Hill |first2=Kenneth D. |title=Systematic studies in the eucalypts - 3. New taxa in ''Eucalyptus'' (Myrtaceae) |journal=Telopea |date=1991 |volume=4 |issue=239–240}}</ref>
* ''Eucalyptus rubida'' subsp. ''barbigerorum'' <small>L.A.S.Johnson & K.D.Hill</small>,<ref name=APC1>{{cite web|title=''Eucalyptus rubida'' subsp. ''barbigerorum''|url= https://biodiversity.org.au/nsl/services/apc-format/display/118671|publisher=Australian Plant Census|access-date=16 December 2019}}</ref> commonly known as blackbutt candlebark,<ref name="CANBR2">{{cite web |title=''Eucalyptus rubida'' subsp. ''barbigerorum'' |url=http://keyserver.lucidcentral.org:8080/euclid/data/02050e02-0108-490e-8900-0e0601070d00/media/Html/Eucalyptus_rubida_subsp._barbigerorum.htm |publisher=Euclid: Centre for Australian National Biodiversity Research |access-date=16 December 2019}}</ref> has elliptic juvenile leaves and a trunk with thick, rough bark at the base;<ref name="RBGS" />
* ''Eucalyptus rubida'' <small>H.Deane & Maiden</small> subsp. ''rubida''<ref name=APC2>{{cite web|title=''Eucalyptus rubida'' subsp. ''rubida''|url= https://biodiversity.org.au/nsl/services/apc-format/display/118669|publisher=Australian Plant Census|access-date=16 December 2019}}</ref> has round juvenile leaves and smooth bark to ground level.<ref name="RBGS" />

==Distribution and habitat==
Candlebark grows in woodland and forest, usually in shallow soils on tablelands, hills and slopes. Subspecies ''barbigerorum'' occurs on the [[Northern Tablelands]] north of [[Armidale, New South Wales|Armidale]]. Subspecies ''rubida'' occurs on the [[Southern Tablelands]] of New South Wales, mainly on the northern side of the [[Great Dividing Range]] in Victoria, between [[Halls Gap]] and [[Delegate, New South Wales|Delegate]], and on the tablelands and mountain slopes of eastern Tasmania.<ref name="CANBR" /><ref name="ABRS" /><ref name="CANBR2" />

==Conservation status==
Subspecies ''barbigerorum'' is classified as "vulnerable" under the Australian Government ''[[Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act 1999]]''. The main threats to the subspecies are habitat disturbance caused by agriculture, development and road work and by timber collection.<ref name="environment">{{cite web |title=Approved Conservation Advice for ''Eucalyptus rubida'' subsp. ''barbigerorum'' |url=http://www.environment.gov.au/biodiversity/threatened/species/pubs/64618-conservation-advice.pdf |publisher=Qustralian Government Department of the Environment |access-date=16 December 2019}}</ref>
